Conclusion We have presented in this paper a set of video distortion metrics that could prove to be particularly useful for HDR video. The main motivating principle we presented was the “spatial detail” signal, which we used in two ways: (1) as a proxy for the original image data and (2) as a guide to the perceptually important features in HDR WCG video. The spatial detail signal is a condensed version of the original image that preserves the recognizable details in an image while discounting local luminance. From a practical standpoint, the important key characteristic of the spatial detail signal is that it is statistically stable having an expectably compact, peaked, biphasic, and symmetric distribution of values that is preserved across a wide range in images and video. Larger values—positive and negative—form a convenient guide to the kinds of features people tend to find significant. The spatial detail values nearer the zero midpoint of the distribution form a convenient guide to image regions that people would tend to classify as background or textural. Such feature and texture maps provide a stable framework in which to selectively investigate the perceptual potent highlights and dark details that are the hallmark of HDR video. Using the spatial detail as a proxy for the original image, we showed that correlation between the spatial detail signals of the uncompressed and compressed versions of HDR video was systematically affected by the aggressiveness of HEVC compression. By combining spatial detail correlation with our feature and texture assignment methods, we showed that texture correlation was impacted significantly more than feature correlation. Spatial detail correlation has several distinctions compared to established video quality metrics. It can be used selectively on bright and dark features and on textures. Moreover, spatial detail values are in the range of 0 to 1, which is more intuitive than the unbounded PSNR scale, while being a much more sensitive indicator than MS-SSIM over the range of compression levels typical of TV services. We have deliberately used the term “video distortion” instead of “video quality” throughout this paper. The main reason for doing so is that the metrics we proposed have not yet been compared to subjective test scores and thus may not yet be claimed to be a calibrated predictor of subjective video quality scores. In addition, it is not the intent of this paper to link the metrics we propose to subjective assessment. Rather,
